concept.name: GraphQL Federation

relationships.description: Connects GraphQL Federation to api gateway in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: GraphQL Federation composes multiple independent domain subgraphs into a single unified schema at a stateless router, letting teams deploy services separately while clients query one endpoint.
spark.keyTakeaway: Federation decouples schema ownership across teams without forcing clients to stitch APIs, provided you enforce strict subgraph composition checks and batch entity lookups.

concept.whyItMatters: As a monolithic GraphQL server grows past 5–10 teams, schema merge conflicts, shared release trains, and coupled database imports stall delivery. Federation moves schema composition to build/registry time and query execution planning to a high-throughput router (such as Apollo Router in Rust or WunderGraph Cosmo), so the Orders team and Identity team ship independently while mobile clients still fetch `user { orders { items { price } } }` in one round trip.
whenToUse: Multiple autonomous backend teams own distinct domain boundaries (e.g., Identity, Catalog, Checkout) and need independent CI/CD pipelines behind one client-facing API.
Mobile or web clients aggregate deeply nested cross-domain data in a single request to avoid client-side waterfall calls over high-latency cellular networks.
You are incrementally strangler-figging a legacy REST or monolithic GraphQL service into domain microservices without breaking existing client queries.
whenNotToUse: A single team owns the entire backend and database; a modular monolith with one GraphQL server avoids network hops, query-planning overhead, and distributed tracing complexity.
Workloads are strictly high-throughput service-to-service RPC or binary streaming where Protobuf over gRPC gives 5–10x lower serialization overhead and strict binary contracts.
Subgraphs share the same underlying relational tables with heavy cross-domain joins; federating across them turns SQL joins into chatty network `_entities` calls.
keyPoints: Subgraphs expose a `_service { sdl }` field and an `_entities(representations: [_Any!]!)` entry point so the router can hydrate foreign types by `@key`.

Federation v2 replaces v1's implicit ownership with explicit directives: `@shareable` for multi-subgraph fields, `@external` + `@requires` for computed cross-subgraph fields, and `@override(from: "...")` for zero-downtime field migrations.

The router compiles each incoming query against the composed supergraph SDL into a static `QueryPlan` (a DAG of `Sequence`, `Parallel`, and `Flatten` fetch steps) before sending a single downstream HTTP request.
Entity resolution batches all parent keys at a given depth into one `_entities` POST per subgraph, preventing per-row N+1 HTTP calls if the subgraph pairs it with DataLoader for its own DB.
Schema checks (`rover subgraph check`) validate composition rules and client traffic impact against persisted operation metrics before a subgraph PR can merge.

examples.title: Cross-subgraph order hydration with @key and @requires
examples.scenario: A Checkout subgraph owns `Order { id totalCents buyerId }` and needs to display `buyer { email }` from Identity plus `shippingEstimateCents` computed from `Product.weightGrams` owned by Catalog.
examples.outcome: Identity defines `type User @key(fields: "id") { id: ID! email: String! }`. Checkout references `extend type User @key(fields: "id") { id: ID! @external }` and marks `Product.weightGrams` as `@external` with `@requires(fields: "weightGrams")` on `shippingEstimateCents`. The router fetches `Order` and `Product.weightGrams` first, then passes `weightGrams` in the `_entities` representation to Checkout.

examples.title: Zero-downtime field migration with @override
examples.scenario: A media platform moves `Video.playbackUrl` from a legacy `Monolith` subgraph to a new `Streaming` subgraph serving 40k RPS without breaking older iOS app versions.
examples.outcome: The `Streaming` subgraph adds `playbackUrl: String! @override(from: "Monolith", label: "percent(10)")` in Federation v2.7+. The router shifts 10% of traffic to `Streaming`, verifies p99 latency and error rates in OpenTelemetry, ramps to `percent(100)`, and then deletes the field from `Monolith`.

tradeOffs.pro: Clients make 1 external round trip instead of 4–6 sequential REST calls, and independent branches in a query execute in `Parallel` at the router.
tradeOffs.con: Deeply nested `@requires` chains create `Sequence` dependencies inside the `QueryPlan`, adding 5–20 ms per hop for router planning, JSON serialization, and internal TLS.

tradeOffs.pro: Teams deploy subgraphs on independent schedules without coordinating a central GraphQL gateway release.
tradeOffs.con: Requires a central schema registry (e.g., Apollo GraphOS or Cosmo Control Plane) and strict linting; an uncoordinated breaking change or `@shareable` conflict can block supergraph composition.

tradeOffs.pro: Automatic Persisted Queries (APQ) at the router let clients send a 64-char SHA-256 hash instead of a 10 KB query string, enabling CDN GET caching for public queries.
tradeOffs.con: Single-endpoint `POST /graphql` defeats URL-based HTTP caching and WAF rules unless query-depth limits, cost analysis, and per-field `@cacheControl` headers are configured.

failureModes.name: Subgraph N+1 database storm
failureModes.description: The router batches 50 `User` keys into a single `_entities(representations: [...])` request, but the subgraph's `__resolveReference` handler issues 50 individual `SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?` queries.
failureModes.mitigation: Wrap every `__resolveReference` and nested field resolver in a request-scoped DataLoader that batches keys into `WHERE id = ANY($1)`.

failureModes.name: Supergraph composition deadlock
failureModes.description: Two teams simultaneously add `status: String` to a shared type without `@shareable`, or rename a `@key` field, causing supergraph composition to fail in CI/CD.
failureModes.mitigation: Run `rover subgraph check` in every subgraph's PR pipeline against the latest production supergraph, and use `@override` or additive deprecations (`@deprecated`) for field moves.

failureModes.name: Cascading partial failure on non-nullable fields
failureModes.description: A non-essential `Reviews` subgraph times out, and because `Product.reviews: [Review!]!` is non-nullable, GraphQL error bubbling nulls out the entire `Product` object.
failureModes.mitigation: Make cross-subgraph extension fields nullable by default, set per-subgraph timeouts (e.g., 800 ms) in the router, and return partial `data` alongside `errors`.

failureModes.name: Query complexity & depth DoS
failureModes.description: An attacker or buggy client sends a cyclic 15-level query (`user { friends { friends { ... } } }`), triggering exponential `_entities` fan-out across subgraphs.
failureModes.mitigation: Enforce static depth limits (e.g., max depth 8), alias limits, and demand-based cost budgets at the router, or lock production to an allowlist of persisted queries.

commonMistakes: Putting business logic or custom resolvers inside the router instead of keeping the router purely declarative for planning, auth, and telemetry.
Splitting a single database across two subgraphs and using `@key` joins over HTTP instead of keeping cohesive tables in one subgraph.
Marking every field `@shareable` to silence composition errors, which causes nondeterministic field resolution if two subgraphs return different values.
Forgetting to propagate `Authorization` and `traceparent` headers from the router to downstream subgraphs, breaking authz and distributed traces.
Allowing unbounded list fields without cursor pagination (`first`/`after`), causing multi-megabyte `_entities` payloads between router and subgraphs.

sections.content:
## The idea

GraphQL Federation separates **schema authoring** from **schema execution**. Each backend service (a *subgraph*) publishes a standard GraphQL schema augmented with federation directives such as `@key`, `@external`, and `@requires`. At build or deploy time, a schema registry composes all subgraph SDLs into a single **supergraph SDL**—verifying that types align, ownership is unambiguous, and every `@key` path is reachable.

At runtime, a stateless **router** (e.g., Apollo Router written in Rust, handling ~10x the RPS per core of a Node.js gateway) receives client queries, parses and validates them against the public API schema, and builds a **QueryPlan**. Rather than executing resolvers one field at a time, the router batches entity references per depth level and dispatches parallel HTTP/gRPC requests to subgraphs' `_entities` endpoints, merging the JSON responses back into the exact shape the client requested.

sections.content:
## Federation v2 directives & composition rules

Federation v1 relied on implicit `extend type` ownership, which broke down when two teams legitimately served the same value object (such as `Money { amount currency }`) or needed to migrate fields without downtime. Federation v2 fixes this with explicit, compiler-checked directives:

- **`@key(fields: "id", resolvable: true)`**: Declares an entity's primary key. Setting `resolvable: false` lets a subgraph reference an entity stub (e.g., `User { id }`) without implementing `__resolveReference`.
- **`@shareable`**: Opts a field or object type into multi-subgraph resolution. Both subgraphs must return semantically identical values for the same input; the router picks whichever subgraph is cheapest to reach in the current `QueryPlan`.
- **`@requires(fields: "weightGrams")` + `@external`**: Tells the query planner that `Checkout` cannot compute `shippingFee` until it receives `weightGrams` from `Catalog`, forcing a `Sequence` edge in the plan.
- **`@provides(fields: "name")`**: Optimization hint declaring that `Orders` already denormalizes `Product.name` in its own table, allowing the router to skip calling `Inventory` when the client only asks for `name`.
- **`@inaccessible`**: Hides internal join keys or migration fields from the public client API schema while keeping them available to the query planner.

sections.eyebrow: 04 / Federation vs. schema stitching vs. BFF
sections.content:
## Federation vs. schema stitching vs. BFF

| Dimension | GraphQL Federation v2 | Manual Schema Stitching | REST / gRPC BFF |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Composition model** | Declarative SDL directives (`@key`, `@requires`) | Imperative gateway resolver code (`delegateToSchema`) | Hand-written aggregation endpoints per screen |
| **Gateway runtime** | Stateless router (Rust / Go), zero business logic | Custom Node.js gateway with team-owned glue code | Custom service per client (iOS, Web) |
| **Type migration** | Built-in `@override(from, label)` traffic splitting | Manual feature flags in gateway code | Duplicate v1/v2 BFF endpoints |
| **N+1 mitigation** | Automatic per-depth `_entities` batching at router | Manual `batchDelegateToSchema` wiring per type | Manual `Promise.all` / goroutine fan-out |
| **Best fit** | 5–50+ microservices with shared domain graph | Legacy GraphQL APIs you cannot add directives to | Tightly coupled UI-specific payloads or low-latency RPC |

## Failure modes

- **Non-nullable error propagation**: In GraphQL, an unhandled error in a non-nullable child field (`orders: [Order!]!`) bubbles up to the nearest nullable ancestor—potentially wiping out the entire `user` payload when one downstream subgraph blips. Always keep cross-subgraph entity fields nullable.
- **QueryPlan explosion**: Unbounded `QueryPlan` compilation on deeply nested polymorphic fragments (`... on TypeA`, `... on TypeB`) can spike router CPU and memory. Cap query depth, limit fragment/alias counts, and size the router's QueryPlan LRU cache (typically 10k–50k entries).
- **Stale supergraph SDL**: If a subgraph deploys a breaking change before the router receives the updated supergraph config, `_entities` queries fail with `400 Bad Request` (`Cannot query field X`). Always gate subgraph deploys on `rover subgraph check` and update the supergraph before removing old fields.
- **Header & auth stripping**: Forgetting to forward `Authorization`, `x-tenant-id`, or `traceparent` in router `headers` rules causes subgraphs to reject valid requests or start disconnected trace roots.

## Governance, telemetry & production hardening

At scale, the router is your single observability choke point. Configure OpenTelemetry export at the router to emit a root span with `graphql.operation.name`, `query_plan.cost`, and child spans per subgraph `Fetch` node—this immediately isolates whether a 400 ms p99 spike is query planning (< 2 ms in Rust), network transit, or a specific subgraph's `_entities` resolver.

Pair observability with **Persisted Query Lists (PQL)** in production: clients ship build-time operation manifests to the registry, and the router rejects arbitrary ad-hoc queries from the public internet. This eliminates runtime query-complexity DoS attacks, shrinks mobile upload payloads to a 64-byte SHA-256 ID, and lets CDNs cache public GET responses at the edge.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Define `@key` fields using immutable internal IDs (UUIDs/ULIDs), never mutable emails or slugs.
- [ ] Implement a request-scoped DataLoader inside every subgraph's `__resolveReference` to batch `_entities` keys into a single DB query.
- [ ] Keep cross-subgraph extension fields nullable so a single subgraph timeout degrades gracefully instead of nulling the root response.
- [ ] Add `rover subgraph check` (or Cosmo `wgc subgraph check`) to every subgraph CI pipeline to block composition breaks and field deletions with active client traffic.
- [ ] Enable Automatic Persisted Queries (APQ) or strict Safelisting + max depth (e.g., 8) and timeout budgets (e.g., 1,000 ms per subgraph) at the router.
- [ ] Forward `traceparent` and verified JWT claims (e.g., `x-user-id` signed/stripped at the edge) to all subgraphs.

interviewProblems.title: GraphQL Federation
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on GraphQL Federation. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: GraphQL Federation composes multiple independent domain subgraphs into a single unified schema at a stateless router, letting teams deploy services separately while clients query one endpoint.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Users Subgraph applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Orders + Inventory.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Orders + Inventory experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Wrap every `__resolveReference` and nested field resolver in a request-scoped DataLoader that batches keys into `WHERE id = ANY($1)`.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Federation decouples schema ownership across teams without forcing clients to stitch APIs, provided you enforce strict subgraph composition checks and batch entity lookups.
Avoid trap: Putting business logic or custom resolvers inside the router instead of keeping the router purely declarative for planning, auth, and telemetry.
Avoid trap: Splitting a single database across two subgraphs and using `@key` joins over HTTP instead of keeping cohesive tables in one subgraph.
When to reach for it: Multiple autonomous backend teams own distinct domain boundaries (e.g., Identity, Catalog, Checkout) and need independent CI/CD pipelines behind one client-facing API.
When to reach for it: Mobile or web clients aggregate deeply nested cross-domain data in a single request to avoid client-side waterfall calls over high-latency cellular networks.

putItTogether.title: Putting Graphql Federation Together
putItTogether.summary: Federation decouples schema ownership across teams without forcing clients to stitch APIs, provided you enforce strict subgraph composition checks and batch entity lookups.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Graphql Federation before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Identity defines `type User @key(fields: "id") { id: ID! email: String! }`. Checkout references `extend type User @key(fields: "id") { id: ID! @external }` and marks `Product.weightGrams` as `@external` with `@requires(fields: "weightGrams")` on `shippingEstimateCents`. The router fetches `Order` and `Product.weightGrams` first, then passes `weightGrams` in the `_entities` representation to Checkout.
